html:
Editing permissions and capabilities

Permissions control whether an otherwise permitted operation runs, asks for approval or is denied. Capabilities control the Skills and tools available to the Agent and how automatic selection chooses them. Enabling a capability does not supply credentials or approve its operations.

In the desktop composer, expand Controls and open Permissions or Capabilities. In Settings, expand Capabilities or Policy / Permissions to edit global defaults directly in the page. The mobile workspace has its own Agent options/policy panels backed by the same server authorities; the desktop dialog layout described below does not apply to every mobile panel.

Choose where the change applies

Scope What an edit changes
This prompt An explicit choice for the next submitted task. Before submission it remains part of the local draft. A permission editor opened for a pending approval can instead target that active request.
This conversation The saved default for that conversation. In a new, unsaved conversation it remains pending intent until the conversation is accepted.
Global The installation's default for conversations that do not override it. Settings limits these editors to this scope.

The active policy can come from a narrower scope than the one you are editing. Check the active/source label before saving. Merely changing the editing scope does not save a policy. A prompt override replaces inherited choices for its scope; it is not automatically merged with every rule from the global editor.

Use inherited permissions/capabilities clears the selected explicit override. At Global scope, Reset to product default restores inheritance from the product default. An explicit empty/default policy and an inherited policy are different choices. In a prompt dialog, the capability editor's Reset button resets its current draft; use Apply to save it. In Settings, resets save automatically.

Global defaults in Settings

Both sections load when first opened and save valid changes automatically after a short pause (350 ms). Closing a section keeps its controls, search and unfinished rule input, and lets pending saves finish. Its heading shows the save status even when collapsed. Searches and disclosure changes do not save; shell rules save when you add or remove them.

These editors always change Global defaults. Conversation and prompt overrides keep their existing precedence. You can continue editing during a save; the latest draft is saved next. If a save fails, the draft stays visible with Retry. A revision conflict stops automatic writes. Reload saved settings discards that pending draft only after the saved settings load successfully.

Permissions

The visible presets are Ask, Custom, Allow and Deny. Ask is the Manual policy: reads normally proceed, while operations needing approval ask. Allow removes routine approval for operations otherwise permitted by the system. Deny applies to permission-gated operations; explicit rules can also restrict reads. Capability limits, hard safety, operating-system permissions and provider authentication still apply. See permission enforcement for precedence and execution details.

Selecting an ordinary preset in the composer saves it for the chosen scope immediately; selecting Custom opens its dialog. Settings edits presets and custom rules inline with autosave. Adding a rule converts the draft to Custom and retains the preset's default decision. In a prompt dialog, choose Apply after editing rules; closing it discards the unsaved editor view. Switching Global permissions to Allow asks for confirmation unless Global is already Allow.

Search finds Skills and tools. Each rule can Allow, Ask, Deny or use Default; Default removes that explicit rule. Skill availability shown here is descriptive: a permission rule does not configure or enable an unavailable Skill.

Shell rules describe executable/subcommand families such as git commit. They do not match arbitrary natural-language intentions, filenames or command arguments. Unsupported families and conflicting duplicate rules are rejected. Use the ordinary approval interaction for one exact operation instead of trying to put its arguments into a persistent family rule.

When a request is awaiting approval, supported Allow/Deny changes can save the selected permission scope and submit that pending decision through the existing approval flow. They are not simply a new unsent prompt preference. Check the request and selected scope before applying the change.

Capabilities

In Automatic mode, Auto keeps a capability eligible for selection, Always includes it in each selection and Never excludes it. Manual mode uses Prefer, Enable and Exclude. Built-in entries are labeled Built in · Always enabled and have no toggle. Runtime controls appear as read-only information. The configuration guide describes automatic selection, built-ins and accepted-task behavior.

The quick menu shows skill/tool switches and marks custom child-tool rules. Unavailable choices cannot be enabled through those switches. The full editor shows more detail, including unavailable reasons and optional configuration links; it can retain preferences for a capability that is unavailable on the current target. Availability is checked for the selected Gateway and conversation, and does not guarantee an operation will execute.

Excluding a Skill clears its child-tool overrides in the draft. Built-in entries remain fixed even when using Clear all or Exclude all others. Shell executable rules use a name such as curl; a simple entered path is reduced to its basename. Arguments such as curl -k are rejected. Excluding one executable does not disable all other ways to perform a similar operation.

Apply validates policy and selection together. Prompt choices stay in the draft; saved conversation/global choices use one revision-checked settings save. The separate Automatic Capability Selection switch in composer Options changes the next prompt locally, while the Settings switch changes the global default. Neither retargets already accepted task intent.

Stale edits and save failures

Shared update notifications refresh effective settings without a dedicated polling loop. An open clean editor can adopt a newer saved choice. Dirty drafts remain visible with a warning, and saves include the revision seen when editing began. If another client changed that saved scope, reopen it to load the latest state before applying your intended edit again.

Changing conversations and restoring a draft invalidate older browser responses. An accepted submission consumes only the local choices that still match its captured draft revision, so an acknowledgement does not normally erase newer edits. Capability catalog responses also check the Gateway/conversation identity before displaying availability.

Closing a dialog is not cancellation of a server write already in progress. If a save fails or its acknowledgement is uncertain, inspect the current effective scope before retrying. The server may have saved a policy before a notification or later read failed. No model call is needed to open, search or preview these editors.
